main_message: Small 2-to-4 unit apartment buildings (like a shop with flats above) basically stopped being built because three sets of rules (zoning, building code stair rules, and bank lending categories) all had to say yes at once and together they make it very hard. Some places are now loosening the first two, but the lending line hasn't moved.
why_hook: The stat of 1 in 13 homes versus 1 in 100 new ones is a clean, surprising contrast, and the question 'why did America stop' is simple. It's a bit numbers-heavy, but I'd stay.
mechanisms_in_your_words: 1) Zoning: most residential land only allows single-family houses, plus parking mandates, going back to the 1920s and the Euclid court case. 2) Building code: more than 3 floors needs two staircases, which eats floor space and adds cost on small lots. 3) Banking: loans are split at 4 units. Mixed shop-plus-apartments and 5+ unit small buildings fall into awkward, harder-to-finance gaps. Together they squeeze out the small building, and the market shifted to single-family houses and big complexes.
ending_comment: Yes, it circles back neatly to the three locks. It does feel slightly like it hedges at the end ('each rule has its defenders'), but it does answer why.

questions_left_unanswered: Why did the 5-19 unit buildings drop so much, and does the bank rule explain that?
What about construction costs, land prices, interest rates, and labor? Do they matter as much as the rules?
Did the older buildings get legally wiped out, or are existing ones still fine?
What does the 'bank line' reform look like and is anyone trying to change it?
Why did larger buildings and single-family houses win in the market, in plain terms?
What would any of this mean for rents or prices where I live?
best_moment: [02] The Euclid story: the four-tier example makes it concrete why a corner shop with flats above ended up illegal in most places, and it has a human quote.
top3_fixes: Cut the stats in 03, 08 and 09 to the few that matter and spell out what each one means in plain words (e.g. 'as of right' = no special permission needed, 'floor plate' = the floor space), so the viewer isn't just handed a list of percentages and cities.

Add a short segment on other causes (construction costs, land prices, interest rates, labor) and say honestly how much the three locks matter relative to them; as is, the 'three locks' thesis feels asserted rather than shown.

Explain the mechanism in 07 and 06: why would a lending gap or a stair rule push builders to big complexes and single-family houses, and add one concrete example of a real small building and how a developer hits all three locks in order.
